doc.title: Paquito D'Rivera — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The minister of culture sends him home to rest
summary: After a year as conductor he got a call telling him to rest for his own safety, and was paid a salary for two years of doing nothing, a paid musical exile.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: So you became the conductor in 1970—
How was your departure from the orchestra determined?

I received a call, a late call from the minister of culture. “Paquito, we decide that the situation is a little complicated these days culturally in the country, and we don’t want you to get hurt here, and I think the best thing you can do, is to go home and rest for a little while, to rest.”

Well, you tell me? “Go to rest.” Huh, I say you want me to go to rest. “Yea, because is complicated everything, and we want you to rest.” Then I went to rest for two years; I did nothing. What they say was even more humiliating, they say, “You don’t have to worry about anything economically. We will pay you a salary every month, and you have all the benefits and everything. You don’t have to worry about money.” So, they pay me a salary every month two years for doing nothing, absolutely nothing.
Would you describe that as a kind of musical exile?
Yea, that’s what is, yea. Yea, it was a paid exile, they pay me every year, every month the salary.
